data_and_models: Two vendor capabilities and one internal asset: Gemini 2.5 Flash, Pro and Flash-Lite via @google/genai for the multimodal read (with automatic failover between the three), Google Search grounding for OEM part-number lookup and live price verification, and a proprietary parts catalog the page sizes at 700,000-plus records across 60-plus makes. Prisma plus PostgreSQL hold estimates and users, Inngest runs the pipeline, R2 or Supabase hold images, Sharp normalises them before inference. No model is trained, and no accuracy, precision or price-error figure is published for either the vision step or the grounding step - the numbers on the page are throughput (under 2 minutes), asset size (700,000 records, 60-plus makes) and band edges (40 and 70 percent), not measurement.
name: Carbender

numbers.arithmetic: not falsifiable from the page: no timing method, device, image count or sample of runs is given, and the call path includes model failover plus live search grounding, so a reader cannot bound the tail a buyer would actually hit
numbers.denominator: damage photos in to priced parts list and repair plan out

numbers.arithmetic: not falsifiable from the page: the catalog is proprietary with no coverage breakdown by make, model or year, so 700,000 rows spread over 60-plus makes and decades of model years says nothing about whether the specific car in the photograph is priced - and every downstream figure, including the Total Loss verdict, depends on that coverage

not falsifiable from the page: a count of makes with no per-make model or year ranges, so it cannot be checked against a buyer's vehicle, and it is the denominator the 700,000-record figure needs in order to mean anything

structural: the formula is stated with both inputs named, so a reader holding the two figures can reproduce the band and the Total Loss call; the band edges themselves are a policy choice, and the appeal to 'EU & US salvage threshold standards' is uncited, with the resale denominator coming from another estimate rather than a transaction record
numbers.claim: Loss Ratio bands: Low <40%, Moderate 40-70%, High >70%
numbers.denominator: Total Estimated Repair Cost divided by Clean Market Resale Value

numbers.arithmetic: structural: countable by opening the product's language settings; nothing about accuracy or coverage depends on it, though the locale list is the only hint of which markets the jurisdiction logic has actually been exercised in

one_line: A salvage-buyer's tool that turns damage photos into a priced OEM parts list, grades severity panel by panel, and divides the repair estimate by clean resale value to say whether the car is worth fixing at all - with US and EU rulebooks treated as different products, and missing parts coverage announced instead of papered over.

sections.accomplishments: A working, paid product is live at carbender.com rather than a hackathon demo, and the author kept shipping after the deadline: five post-hackathon updates in the 45 days since the project started, at 39, 34, 30, 26 and 16 days before the read, including the window-sticker generator. The end-to-end path - photo in, priced OEM parts list, severity grades and repair-plan PDF out - is described as running in under 2 minutes. No accuracy figure for any of it is published.
sections.challenges: Coverage is the stated problem, and the page treats it as a design constraint rather than an edge case: it describes scarcity detection and advisory banners whose job is to communicate the limits of the parts catalog honestly instead of returning empty or misleading results, with the operating principle stated plainly - a wrong OEM code shown with false confidence is worse than showing no result. The second named difficulty is jurisdiction: two standards bodies, two currencies, and per-country import, title, emissions and inspection rules that have to be attached to the right estimate rather than translated after the fact, which is also what pulls Stripe multi-currency into the stack.
sections.how_we_built_it: Next.js App Router with TypeScript, Tailwind and React on the front; Prisma over PostgreSQL (Neon) for state, Cloudflare R2 or Supabase for media, Sharp for image preparation, and Inngest for the asynchronous estimate pipeline. Stripe carries multi-currency billing. Recognition and pricing run on Gemini 2.5 Flash, Pro and Flash-Lite through @google/genai, with automatic failover between the three models, and Google Search grounding is used to look up OEM part numbers and verify live prices. Nothing is trained; the parts catalog the page calls proprietary, at 700,000-plus records across 60-plus vehicle makes, is presented as an asset rather than as something built here, and its construction is not documented.
sections.inspiration: The page frames the gap as an information problem at the moment of bidding: a salvage buyer sees photographs of damage and has no way to price them, so the bid is a guess about part availability, labour and whether the car is repairable at all. The two structures the product adds on top of vision - a severity grade per panel and a repair-cost-to-resale ratio with published bands - are both attempts to turn that guess into a number a buyer can argue with. The region split in the same breath (DOT/SAE and USD against ECE and EUR, with per-country import, title, emissions and inspection warnings) says the missing piece is not only recognition but the paperwork and pricing context around a wreck.
sections.learned: The lesson the page argues hardest is presentational honesty under incomplete data: when the catalog does not cover a vehicle, say so in the interface, because a confident wrong part number is worse than an admitted blank. The second is that region is not a translation layer - standards family, currency, title rules and inspection requirements change what the estimate means, so the product is built as two jurisdictions with one vision core. The third is operational: three Gemini model tiers with automatic failover, because a single inference endpoint is a downtime dependency in a flow a buyer is running against an auction clock.
sections.what_it_does: Photos go in and a structured estimate comes out: damaged parts identified against an OEM catalog, each graded Severe, Moderate or Cosmetic, with 3D spatial normalisation used to tell driver-side from passenger-side damage rather than trusting the photo's left and right. Every identified part carries a real-market price report, and the parts assemble into a Repair Planner that exports a PDF. A Loss Ratio - Total Estimated Repair Cost divided by Clean Market Resale Value - is banded Low under 40 percent, Moderate 40 to 70, High above 70, described as matching EU and US salvage threshold standards, and a High ratio returns a Total Loss verdict. Jurisdiction changes the vocabulary (US DOT/SAE standards and USD, EU ECE in EUR) and adds country-aware import, title, emissions and inspection warnings. A separate free tool at carbender.com/window-sticker turns a VIN into a Monroney window sticker, and the whole product is a zero-download mobile web app in four locales (English, Lithuanian, Polish and US English).
sections.what_next: The page publishes no roadmap section; the observable trajectory is product maintenance - five updates after the deadline, one of them an adjacent free tool - and the gaps it leaves are the ones a buyer would ask about first: no error rate for part identification, no calibration for the repair estimate, no coverage table by make, model and year behind the 700,000-record catalog, and no source named for the 'matching EU & US salvage threshold standards' claim attached to the Loss Ratio bands. What exists to be extended is the verdict layer: the bands and the Total Loss call are the only place the product tells a user what to do.

testing: No evaluation of any kind is described: no precision or recall on part identification, no back-test of repair estimates against shop invoices or auction outcomes, no error bars on the Loss Ratio, no hold-out by make or model year, and no mention of a test suite. The only quantitative structure on the page is the Loss Ratio band policy - Low under 40 percent, Moderate 40 to 70, High above 70 - which is a threshold choice presented as matching 'EU & US salvage threshold standards' with no citation for either standard. The honesty device the page does describe is in the interface rather than in a benchmark: scarcity detection and advisory banners that flag where the catalog does not reach.
